terms.definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol — the language browsers and servers use to request and deliver web pages and API data.
terms.example: When you visit a URL, your browser sends an HTTP GET request; the server responds with status 200 and the page HTML.

terms.definition: Representational State Transfer — an API style that uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources identified by URLs.
terms.example: GET /users/42 returns user 42. POST /users creates a new user.

terms.definition: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations on persistent data.
terms.example: A blog API supports CRUD on posts: POST to create, GET to read, PUT to update, DELETE to remove.

terms.definition: A performance bug where fetching N items triggers N additional database queries instead of one batched query.
terms.example: Loading 100 users then querying each user's posts individually = 1 + 100 queries.

terms.definition: A thin end-to-end feature cut through all layers (UI → API → DB) that delivers user value on its own.
terms.example: 'User can reset password' is a vertical slice; 'build the database layer' is not.

terms.definition: Observable conditions that must be true for a feature to be considered done.
terms.example: Given a valid email, when user clicks reset, then they receive a link within 60 seconds.

terms.definition: The underlying reason a failure occurred — not the symptom, but the condition that made the symptom possible.
terms.example: Symptom: 500 errors. Root cause: missing null check when user has no profile photo.

terms.definition: The ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs: logs, metrics, and traces.
terms.example: A spike in 500s plus error logs showing 'connection refused' points to a database outage.

terms.definition: A fast storage layer that keeps copies of frequently accessed data to avoid expensive recomputation or remote fetches.
terms.example: Redis caches user sessions so every request doesn't hit the database.

terms.definition: An operation that produces the same result no matter how many times it's executed.
terms.example: DELETE /items/5 is idempotent — calling it twice still leaves item 5 deleted.
